_comment: Generic bashguard base rules: commands that hang a headless agent shell (interactive editors, pagers, unbounded poll loops). See engine.ts for the matcher vocabulary. Site-specific layers are merged on top by ~/.pi/agent/bashguard/local.ts (or BASHGUARD_RULES); later layers replace rules by id.

rules.reason: pgrep -f inside a while poll matches the loop's own command line (the pattern is part of it), so the loop never exits and hangs the session. Poll with pgrep -x <binary>, bracket-escape the pattern (e.g. 'jobs_all[.]txt'), or check output-file growth with bounded sleeps instead.

pgrep -f inside an until poll matches the loop's own command line (the pattern is part of it), giving an instant false success or a hang. Poll with pgrep -x <binary>, bracket-escape the pattern (e.g. 'jobs_all[.]txt'), or check output-file growth with bounded sleeps instead.

git rebase -i opens an interactive editor and hangs a headless shell. Use a non-interactive alternative (e.g. git rebase --onto, git commit --fixup + rebase --autosquash with GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true) or ask the user.
git add -p/-i/-e is interactive and hangs a headless shell. Stage whole files, or build a partial change in a temp file instead.
git commit/merge/revert without a message flag opens an interactive editor and hangs a headless shell. Pass -m '<msg>' (or --no-edit where applicable).
crontab -e opens an interactive editor and hangs a headless shell. Use 'crontab -l' to read and 'crontab <file>' to install a new table.
visudo opens an interactive editor and hangs a headless shell. Ask the user to edit sudoers.
vim is interactive and hangs a headless shell. Use your file read/edit tools instead.
nvim is interactive and hangs a headless shell (headless test runs with --headless are allowed; wrap them in 'timeout'). Use your file read/edit tools instead.
vi is interactive and hangs a headless shell. Use your file read/edit tools instead.
nano is interactive and hangs a headless shell. Use your file read/edit tools instead.
emacs without --batch/--script is interactive and hangs a headless shell. Use your file read/edit tools instead.
less is an interactive pager and hangs a headless shell. Pipe to 'head -n N' or 'cat', or read the file directly.
more is an interactive pager and hangs a headless shell. Pipe to 'head -n N' or 'cat', or read the file directly.
Dumping .env files puts secrets into the agent context and logs. Read .env.example/.env.sample for the variable names, or ask the user for the specific value you need.
Dumping private key material puts secrets into the agent context and logs. Public halves (*.pub) are fine; for anything else, ask the user.

Uploading a local file to a URL (curl -d @file / -F x=@file / -T file) is the exfiltration chokepoint: once data is laundered into another file the guard can't tell what's in it. If this is a legitimate upload, ask the user to run it (or to allow-list it).
wget --post-file/--body-file uploads a local file to a URL — an exfiltration chokepoint. If this is a legitimate upload, ask the user to run it.

Raw network pipes (nc/ncat/socat/telnet) can stream local data to an arbitrary host and bypass normal tooling. Port checks (nc -z) and listeners (-l) are allowed; for anything else use the proper client (curl to a known endpoint) or ask the user.
Copying files to a remote host (scp/sftp/rsync to user@host:path) is an exfiltration chokepoint. Local copies are unaffected; for a real remote transfer, ask the user.
That file holds credentials; dumping it puts secrets into the agent context and logs. Ask the user for the specific value you need.
